sources.title: Ichthyophthirius multifiliis (White Spot) Infections in Fish
Fish Fungal Infections: 3 Common Types and Treatments

Hình ảnh các loại thuốc trị bệnh cho cá

facts.fact: White spot disease (Ich) is caused by the ciliate protozoan Ichthyophthirius multifiliis. It affects freshwater aquarium fish and farmed fish.
Ich can cause rapid, high mortality. One parasite can produce up to 1,024 offspring in one generation.
Ich completes its life cycle on fish without a second host. Adult parasites leave the fish, encyst in the tank and release many free-swimming infective stages.
Only the free-swimming theront stage can be killed by treatment. Parasites on the fish are shielded by the fish's skin and mucus.
At 75–79°F, the Ich life cycle takes about 3 to 6 days. In cool water it takes weeks.
Saprolegnia and other Oomycota, often called fish 'fungus', are fungus-like protists rather than true fungi.
Aquatic fungi are usually secondary invaders. They follow injury, infection, poor water quality or low water temperature, and many grow on decaying organic matter.
Ich shows as small white spots or salt-grain-like dots on the skin and fins.
Early Ich signs, before spots appear, include flashing (rubbing against objects), extra mucus, lethargy and poor appetite.
Other Ich signs include clamped fins and darker colour.
Gill-only Ich infections may show no spots. Gills look pale and swollen, and many fish can die.
When gills are infected, fish may breathe rapidly or gasp at the surface.
White spots alone should never be used to diagnose Ich, because other diseases look similar. Confirm by examining skin, gill or fin samples under a microscope.
Lymphocystis and some sporozoan infections can look like white spot disease.
Velvet (Piscinoodinium) in freshwater fish gives a brownish-gold, rust or gold-dust look, with small golden spots rather than white ones.
Fungal or water-mould infections look like fuzzy, cotton-like white, tan or yellowish patches on the body, fins, eyes or gills.
Bacterial infections such as columnaris, and damaged tissue, can look like fungus.
Columnaris (Flavobacterium columnare) can appear as creamy material on goldfish gills and as 'haystacks' of bacteria on Corydoras skin. A microscope wet mount shows many filamentous, motile bacteria.
Ich can be brought in with new fish, substrates, plants or equipment.
Ich spreads from infected water or newly added infected fish and is highly contagious.
Water mist or spray can carry Ich between nearby tanks.
Fungal infections are linked to poor water quality, waste buildup, overcrowding, aggressive tank mates, skin or fin injuries, and dead fish left in the tank.
Columnaris is most common in warmwater species.
If even one Ich parasite is found, start treatment immediately. As the infection advances, fish may die even with treatment.
For fungal infections, correct the stressors first: water quality, diet, overcrowding and aggression. Mild cases may improve once these are fixed.
Remove dead fish quickly. Ich parasites leave dead fish and multiply in the tank.
Ich salt treatment: a prolonged bath of 4 to 5 g/L for 7 to 10 days at 75–79°F, for smaller systems.
Merck lists raising salinity to 5 g/L for one week at 24°C or higher as a freshwater Ich treatment, if the species tolerates it.
Most freshwater fish tolerate 5 ppt salt for several weeks. Salt tolerance varies by species, so check each species' limits.
Aquarium plants and small-pond plants may not tolerate raised salinity.
VCA says salt treatment is suitable only for scaled fish. Use aquarium salt, not table salt, and remove it afterwards with several water changes.
Ich formalin treatment: 25 mg/L (1 mL per 10 gallons). Formalin-sensitive species get half that, 12.5 mg/L.
Give strong aeration during formalin treatment, especially if gills are damaged. If fish look stressed or try to jump, flush with clean, oxygenated water.
Copper sulfate dose for Ich (mg/L) = total alkalinity (mg/L) ÷ 100. Do not use it if alkalinity is below 50 mg/L. An overdose kills fish.
UF/IFAS does not recommend potassium permanganate for Ich. Using it more than once a week damages skin, gills and eyes.
Ich treatment schedule at 75–79°F: treat daily, at least 3 to 5 treatments. At 60°F, space treatments 3 to 5 days apart, at least 5 treatments.
Merck: at warm aquarium temperatures (above 26°C), treat Ich daily for 3 to 7 treatments. Formalin or copper are the drugs of choice.
Most Ich strains cannot survive above 86°F (30°C). Raise the temperature slowly and add oxygen, because not all fish tolerate heat.
Sera advises raising the temperature slightly for a few days for white spot, with about 31°C (88°F) as ideal if the fish tolerate it. Afterwards, lower it slowly.
Sera costapur for white spot: treat on days 1 and 3, and again on days 5 and 7 if new spots appear. Keep lights off on treatment days and aerate well.
Some invertebrates are sensitive to sera's white spot treatment, so sera suggests using a quarantine tank.
Cartilaginous fish such as sharks and rays do not tolerate malachite green or similar compounds.
Malachite green is effective against Ich and is in many over-the-counter products. Merck says vets should not dispense it because of regulatory concerns, and it must never be used on food fish.
Moving fish to a clean, uninfected tank every 24 hours can clear Ich within a few days. Colder water needs longer.
An 80-micron mesh filter can remove Ich stages from the water.
For freshwater fungal infections, aquarium salt at 1–2 g/L may reduce fungal growth. Measure it accurately and keep salinity stable during water changes.
Severe fungal infections such as Branchiomyces are hard to treat, and humane euthanasia may be recommended.

For bacterial hemorrhagic septicemia (Aeromonas, Pseudomonas), first remove causes such as low oxygen, poor water and handling stress. Use antibiotics if fish are dying, chosen by sensitivity testing where possible.
Merck: no effective treatment eliminates mycobacteria (fish tuberculosis), and the infection can pass to people handling fish.
Metronidazole is the only available treatment for the intestinal flagellate Spironucleus in ornamental fish. Give it orally, or as a bath if fish will not eat.
Ich steps: confirm the diagnosis, treat repeatedly on a schedule set by temperature, clean the tank daily to remove cysts in debris, and continue until deaths stop.
Quarantine all new fish for at least 30 days. Ich can appear 1 to 3 weeks after shipping in warm water.
Before adding plants, substrate or decorations, hold them without fish for one life cycle at current temperature, or disinfect them.
Do not share nets or siphons between tanks unless they have been disinfected.
Fungus prevention: clean water tested regularly for ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, a balanced diet, no overcrowding, and managed aggression.
Leaving a tank empty of fish (fallow) breaks the Ich cycle. Cysts resist chemicals, so clean gravel and debris thoroughly.
A common mistake is giving a single Ich treatment or stopping too early. Treatment must be repeated until deaths stop.
Fish that recover from Ich can carry the infection to other fish.
Using copper sulfate without testing alkalinity is a common error. It is extremely toxic to fish in low-alkalinity water.
Moving fish to a hospital tank for 48 hours lets parasites in the main tank die off, but this alone does not cure Ich.
Natural methods are less reliable than chemical treatment for Ich, and resistant strains can develop.
Vietnamese shops call Ich 'bệnh đốm trắng' ('cá bị đốm trắng'). They mention methylene blue ('xanh methylen'), malachite green and non-iodized salt as treatments.

A Vietnamese forum keeper reports buying tetracycline, potassium permanganate ('thuốc tím'), metronidazole, ampicillin, tinidazole and ciprofloxacin at human pharmacies ('tiệm thuốc tây') to treat fish.
The same Vietnamese keeper reports 'Tetra Nhật' antibiotic powder and BIOFISH digestive probiotic ('men tiêu hóa') sold in fish shops.
Calling every white spot 'Ich' is wrong, say UF/IFAS and sera: lymphocystis, sporozoans and other diseases look similar.
Fish 'fungus' is mostly not true fungus: PetMD's vet author says it is often water moulds, and Merck classes Saprolegnia as fungus-like protists.
